ru: В лаборато́рии стоя́т но́вые аппара́ты.
en: There is new apparatus in the laboratory.
note: English "apparatus" is a mass noun; the count plural "apparatuses" is what no one writes. The uncountable reading also keeps the headword visible, where "machines" would hide it.

ru: С утра́ бы́ло я́сно и безо́блачно.
en: It had been clear and cloudless since morning.
note: "Since morning it was" mixes a since-adverbial with a simple past, which English does not do. The past perfect is what carries с утра́ up to the moment described.

ru: До́ма гото́вят вкусне́е, чем в кафе́.
en: At home they cook better than in a cafe.
note: "They cook tastier food" fixed the adverb and left an object the Russian never had. English keeps the impersonal plural and the bare comparative adverb; "better" is what an English speaker says of cooking, and it costs the вкус- root, which is the smaller loss against inventing "food".

ru: Дед горди́тся свои́ми вну́ками бо́льше всего́ на све́те.
en: Grandad is proud of his grandsons more than anything in the world.
note: "The grandfather" as a bare definite is not how English names a family member; дед is Grandad. The rest of the sentence was already right.

ru: При но́вой рабо́те бу́дут возника́ть тру́дности.
en: Difficulties will keep arising in a new job.
note: Fronting the adverbial is a Russian word order that English only uses for contrast. Nothing here is contrasted, so the adverbial belongs at the end.

ru: Без сове́та я бы выбира́ла до́лго.
en: Without advice it would take me a long time to choose.
note: "I would take a long time choosing" is grammatical but not what is said; the impersonal "it would take me" is the English frame, and the imperfective's drawn-out reading survives it.

ru: Она́ вы́разила благода́рность сло́вом.
en: She expressed her gratitude in words.
note: "With a word" reads as a single utterance; "in a word" would mean "to sum up". The instrumental сло́вом is the means — words rather than deeds — which "in words" carries.

ru: В кни́ге пи́шут о жи́зни домохозя́ек.
en: The book is about the lives of housewives.
note: "In the book they write about" transliterates the impersonal plural instead of translating it. English makes the book the subject. Also "lives", since each housewife has one.

ru: Жа́лко тра́тить вре́мя зря.
en: It is a pity to spend time for nothing.
note: "Waste ... for nothing" says the same thing twice — waste already means for nothing. тра́тить is neutral "spend", and зря supplies the futility once.

ru: От бо́ли он бы заора́л на весь дом.
en: He would start yelling in pain for the whole house to hear.
note: "In pain he would start yelling" fronts the cause the way От бо́ли does; English puts it after the verb unless it is being contrasted.

ru: От оби́ды я бы запла́кал.
en: I would have burst into tears out of hurt.
note: "From the hurt" is the Russian preposition carried across. English takes "out of" for an emotion as cause.

ru: Мы зря потра́тили вре́мя.
en: We spent our time for nothing.
note: "Wasted ... for nothing" is tautologous — the same doubling as жа́лко тра́тить вре́мя зря. потра́тить is "spent"; зря is what makes it wasted.

ru: Они́ извиня́т нас за опозда́ние пото́м.
en: Afterwards they will excuse us for being late.
note: Sentence-final "afterwards" attaches to "being late", saying they were late afterwards. Fronting пото́м removes the ambiguity.

ru: Из ку́хни вку́сно па́хнет.
en: There is a delicious smell coming from the kitchen.
note: English needs the participle: a smell is not "from" somewhere, it comes from there. The bare prepositional phrase is the Russian construction.

ru: На перегово́рах она́ держа́лась с незнако́мыми мужчи́нами уве́ренно.
en: At the negotiations she conducted herself confidently with men she did not know.
note: "The unfamiliar men" reads as a definite group already introduced, which незнако́мыми does not say — it says she did not know them.

ru: Ско́ро всё ока́жется на свои́х места́х.
en: Soon everything will be in its proper place.
note: "End up in its place" implies a haphazard landing; "fall into place" would mean it starts making sense. на свои́х места́х is simply where each thing belongs.

ru: Я очну́сь от шу́ма.
en: I will come round at the noise.
note: "Come to because of the noise" is not a collocation English has — "come to" does not take a because-clause for its trigger. English takes "at" for the stimulus one comes round at, which keeps «я» as the subject; making the noise the subject would fix the English by losing the person.

ru: Учёные говоря́т о ле́дниковом пери́оде.
en: Scientists are talking about the Ice Age.
note: "The glacial period" is a technical term a geologist might use; ледниковый период is the ordinary name for it, which in English is the Ice Age.

ru: Го́сти до́лго аплоди́ровали повара́м за у́жин.
en: The guests gave the cooks a long round of applause for the dinner.
note: "Spent a long time applauding ... for the dinner" stacks two adjuncts that fight each other. The English idiom folds до́лго into the applause itself.

ru: В кни́ге пи́шут о вели́ких проро́ках.
en: The book is about great prophets.
note: Same impersonal plural as the домохозя́йка sentence: English makes the book the subject rather than reporting what unnamed people write in it.

ru: Пья́ная компа́ния шуме́ла во дворе́.
en: A drunken group was making a noise in the yard.
note: British English takes the article — "making a noise". The imperfective шуме́ла is a stretch of noise rather than one event, so the progressive.

ru: За рулём сиди́т о́пытный води́тель.
en: An experienced driver sits behind the wheel.
note: "Behind the steering wheel" is redundant: English "behind the wheel" already means driving, and за рулём is exactly that idiom.

ru: При друго́м реше́нии судьба́ сложи́лась бы ина́че.
en: Fate would have turned out differently with a different decision.
note: Fronting При друго́м реше́нии is Russian word order; English states the outcome first and the condition after.

ru: Он де́лает всё, что уго́дно.
en: He does anything you like.
note: "Anything at all" as an object of a bare present makes the sentence read as a complaint about indiscriminate behaviour. «всё, что уго́дно» offers, and уго́дный is what supplies the "you like".
